claim: Federal basic exclusion amount for decedents dying in 2027
source: IRS news release IR-2026-133 (Nov. 5, 2026); Rev. Proc. 2026-35 sec. 3.44
evidence: 'Estates of decedents who die during 2027 have a basic exclusion amount of $15,480,000, up from a total of $15,000,000 for estates of decedents who died in 2026.'
notes: Published 6 days before this check; earlier sessions could not have had it. Implied one-year index: +3.2%.

claim: Annual gift tax exclusion per recipient

claim: Form 706 filing thresholds by year of death, 2011-2026
source: IRS - Estate tax (filing threshold table)
evidence: Table 'Filing threshold for year of death' reproduced row by row.

claim: What is counted against the threshold
value: Gross estate (cash, securities, real estate, insurance, trusts, annuities, business interests) at fair market value, plus adjusted taxable gifts made since 1977; less debts, administration expenses, marital and charitable deductions
source: IRS - Estate tax
evidence: 'The fair market value of these items is used... The includible property may consist of cash and securities, real estate, insurance, trusts, annuities, business interests and other assets.'

claim: Form 706 due date and extension; portability election
value: Due 9 months after death; automatic 6-month extension with Form 4768; portability (DSUE) only by timely filed Form 706; late portability relief up to the 5th anniversary under Rev. Proc. 2022-32 when no filing was otherwise required
source: IRS - Frequently asked questions on estate taxes
evidence: 'The due date of the estate tax return is nine months after the decedent's date of death, however, the estate's representative may request an extension of time to file the return for up to six months.'

claim: 2027 long-term capital gain rate breakpoints
value: 0% up to $51,050 single / $102,100 joint; 15% up to $563,200 single / $633,600 joint / $598,400 head of household; 20% above; estates and trusts reach 20% above $16,750
source: Rev. Proc. 2026-35 sec. 3.03
evidence: Table 'Maximum Zero Rate Amount / Maximum 15% Rate Amount' reproduced.

claim: 2027 income tax brackets for estates and trusts
source: Rev. Proc. 2026-35 sec. 3.01 Table 5
evidence: Table 5 - Estates and Trusts reproduced.

claim: 2027 top individual rate and thresholds
source: IRS news release IR-2026-133
evidence: Marginal rates list reproduced.

claim: Capital gain rate structure and depreciation-related gain
value: 0% / 15% / 20% on net long-term gain; unrecaptured section 1250 gain taxed at a maximum 25%; short-term gain taxed as ordinary income; personal-use losses not deductible
source: IRS Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses
evidence: 'The portion of any unrecaptured section 1250 gain from selling section 1250 real property is taxed at a maximum 25% rate.' 'Losses from the sale of personal-use property, such as your home or car, aren't tax deductible.'

claim: California estate tax return requirement
value: None for deaths on or after January 1, 2005
source: California State Controller - California Estate Tax
evidence: 'For decedents that die on or after January 1, 2005, there is no longer a requirement to file a California Estate Tax Return.'

claim: California inheritance tax and gift tax
value: Collected only for deaths / gifts before June 8, 1982
source: California State Controller - California Estate Tax
evidence: 'For decedents that died prior to June 8, 1982, the State Controller's Office will continue to collect the Inheritance Tax.'

claim: Prop 19 adjusted $1 million amount by transfer date
source: BOE Letter to Assessors No. 2025/009 (March 7, 2025); 2026 LTA index checked 12 Nov 2026
evidence: Enclosure table reproduced. 'The next adjustment of the $1 million amount will occur in February 2027.' Re-checked BOE 2026 LTA index (https://www.boe.ca.gov/proptaxes/2026.htm, 2026/001-2026/044) on 12 Nov 2026: no Feb 2027 cap adjustment issued yet.
notes: Adjustment uses the FHFA House Price Index for California for the prior calendar year (2.15% for 2024). The post-Feb-2027 amount is not yet published as of Nov 12, 2026.

claim: Prop 19 family-home conditions
value: Home must be the parent's principal residence and become the child's principal residence within one year of the transfer; no exceptions
source: BOE Letter to Assessors No. 2026/026 (August 3, 2026), Q7
evidence: 'the transfer is required to be of a principal residence of the transferor that qualifies as the principal residence of the transferee within one year after the transfer under section 63.2(a)(1)(A). There are no exceptions to this rule.'

claim: Prop 19 value cap and new taxable value formula
value: Cap = factored base year value + adjusted $1 million. If market value exceeds the cap, the excess is added to the factored base year value. New taxable value then grows by the annual inflation factor.
source: BOE Letter to Assessors No. 2026/026, 'Value Cap' and Q49-Q51
evidence: 'If the full cash value on the date of transfer exceeds the value cap, the amount above the value cap is added to the factored base year value, resulting in a new taxable value.' Worked example Q50: FBYV $163,076, FMV $1,200,000, cap $1,163,076, excess $36,924.

claim: Prop 19 filing deadlines
value: Homeowners' (or Disabled Veterans') Exemption claim within 1 year of transfer; exclusion claim within 3 years of transfer or before transfer to a third party, whichever is earlier; otherwise prospective relief only
source: BOE Letter to Assessors No. 2026/026, 'Filing Requirements'
evidence: 'the transferee must file for the Homeowners' or Disabled Veterans' Exemption within one year of the date of purchase or transfer to be considered timely. The transferee must also file for the appropriate intergenerational transfer exclusion within three years...'

claim: What happens if the heir later moves out or rents the home
value: Exclusion is removed; the value enrolled on the next lien date is the market value at the date of the original transfer, factored for inflation since then (not the then-current market value)
source: BOE Letter to Assessors No. 2026/026, 'Continual Use Requirement' and Q8, Q53
evidence: 'The value to be enrolled on the lien date following the date the exclusion no longer qualifies is the full cash value established as of the change in ownership date (new base year value), adjusted annually for inflation (factored)...'

claim: Transfers through a trust
value: Eligible; the trust is looked through to the beneficial owner; no requirement on how title names the occupant
source: BOE Letter to Assessors No. 2026/026, Q39-Q40
evidence: 'for property tax purposes, the trust must be looked through to determine who has present beneficial ownership... transfers of property held in a trust are eligible for the exclusion.'

claim: Rental or other non-principal-residence property
value: No parent-child exclusion; reassessed to market value at the date of transfer. A rented home is not eligible for the Homeowners' Exemption.
source: BOE Proposition 19 page (comparison chart) and LTA 2026/026 Q2, Q31
evidence: Chart: 'Eliminates exclusion for other real property other than the principal residence'. Q31: 'section 218(b) provides that the exemption does not extend to rented property.'

claim: More than one child inheriting
value: If the trust or will lets the trustee distribute non-pro-rata, the home can go to one child and still be excluded provided its value does not exceed that child's share of the whole estate; a later buy-out between siblings is a reassessable sibling transfer
source: BOE Letter to Assessors No. 2026/026, Q41-Q42
evidence: 'if the market value of the family home does not exceed that child's share of the entire estate, then the distribution of real property to one child may be excluded' ; sibling swaps 'would trigger a 50% reappraisal of each parcel.'
notes: Number of beneficiaries of the trust is not stated in the household record - flagged.

claim: Basis of inherited property (step-up)
value: Generally fair market value on the date of death (or the alternate valuation date if elected on Form 706). Selling for more than that basis is a taxable gain.
source: IRS FAQ - Gifts & inheritances
evidence: 'The basis of property inherited from a decedent is generally one of the following: The fair market value (FMV) of the property on the date of the decedent's death (whether or not the executor of the estate files an estate tax return...'

claim: Main-home sale exclusion
value: Up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 joint) if owned and used as main home for at least 24 months of the 5 years before sale
source: IRS Topic no. 701, Sale of your home
evidence: 'you may qualify to exclude up to $250,000 of that gain from your income, or up to $500,000 of that gain if you file a joint return with your spouse.'
notes: Amounts are fixed in statute and not inflation-indexed.

claim: Net investment income tax
value: 3.8% on the lesser of net investment income or MAGI above $200,000 (single / head of household) or $250,000 (joint). Applies to rents and gains on real estate and securities; not to home-sale gain that is excluded. Thresholds are not indexed.
source: IRS Topic no. 559, Net investment income tax
evidence: 'A 3.8 percent net investment income tax (NIIT) applies to individuals, estates, and trusts that have net investment income above applicable threshold amounts.'

claim: Rental income and deductible expenses
value: Rent is ordinary income on Schedule E; depreciation, repairs and operating expenses are deductible; rental profit can be subject to NIIT; losses are limited by passive-activity rules
source: IRS Topic no. 414, Rental income and expenses
evidence: 'Depreciation - ... You begin to depreciate your rental property when you place it in service.' 'If you have a rental profit, you may be subject to the net investment income tax (NIIT).'
notes: Residential rental recovery period (27.5 years) is in Publication 527; not re-opened this session - flagged.

claim: California treatment of capital gains

source: Franchise Tax Board - Capital gains and losses
evidence: 'California does not have a lower rate for capital gains. All capital gains are taxed as ordinary income.'

claim: How the Prop 19 $1 million amount is indexed
value: Every second February 16 the amount is multiplied by ONE year's change in the FHFA House Price Index for California (the prior calendar year only). 2023: x 1.0226 (2022 change) = $1,022,600. 2025: x 1.0215 (2024 change) = $1,044,586. The intervening year's change is not applied.
source: BOE Letters to Assessors No. 2023/012 (March 7, 2023) and No. 2025/009 (March 7, 2025)
evidence: 'the annual percentage change in the House Price Index for California for 2022 was 2.26 percent. Accordingly, the $1 million amount is adjusted to $1,022,600.' ; 'for 2024 was 2.15 percent. Accordingly, the $1 million amount is adjusted to $1,044,586.'
notes: Consequence: the excluded amount grows at roughly half the pace of home prices, so the share of an expensive home that Prop 19 shelters shrinks over time. The site model on main compounded two years of growth per step, which overstates the future amount - corrected at integration and flagged.

value: Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return
source: IRS - Topic no. 701, Sale of your home
evidence: 'you may qualify to exclude up to $250,000 of that gain from your income, or up to $500,000 of that gain if you file a joint return with your spouse'; 'owned the home for at least 24 months (2 years) out of the last 5 years leading up to the date of the sale'. Opened 11 Nov 2026.
notes: The exclusion covers gain only; an inherited house starts with almost no gain.

claim: Rental real estate losses are generally passive, carried forward, and released when the whole interest is sold
value: Carried forward; fully deductible in the year of disposition
source: IRS - Topic no. 425, Passive activities
evidence: 'In general, rental activities, including rental real estate activities, are passive activities even if you materially participate.' 'You can carry forward disallowed passive losses to the next taxable year.' 'Generally, you may fully deduct any previously disallowed passive activity loss in the year you dispose of your entire interest in the activity.' Opened 11 Nov 2026.
notes: Used for the depreciation test on the Other options page.

claim: Gain from depreciation on real property is taxed at a maximum 25% federal rate; land is never depreciable
value: 25% maximum; residential rental GDS period 27.5 years
source: IRS - Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses; Topic no. 704, Depreciation; Publication 527
evidence: Topic 409: 'The portion of any unrecaptured section 1250 gain from selling section 1250 real property is taxed at a maximum 25% rate.' Topic 704 (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc704): 'Land is never depreciable'. Publication 527 (https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527, opened 12 Nov 2026): Table 2-1 lists residential rental property GDS recovery period as 27.5 years straight-line mid-month.
notes: Publication 527 directly opened and verified 12 Nov 2026 (see N-12).

claim: Section 1031 applies only to real property held for business or investment
value: No gain recognised on a qualifying exchange; money received is taxed
source: IRS - Like-kind exchanges, real estate tax tips
evidence: 'when you exchange real property used for business or held as an investment solely for other business or investment property that is the same type'; 'you must recognize a gain to the extent of the other property and money received'. Opened 11 Nov 2026.
notes: Not modelled.

claim: Most non-spouse heirs must empty an inherited retirement account within ten years; distributions are income
value: End of the 10th year after the year of death
source: IRS - Retirement topics, Beneficiary
evidence: 'Beneficiaries must include any taxable distributions they receive in their gross income.' 'Designated beneficiary (not an eligible designated beneficiary) - Follow the 10-year rule'. '10-year rule: ... Empty the entire account by the end of the 10th year following the year of the account owner's ... death'. 'Withdrawals of contributions from an inherited Roth are tax free.' Opened 11 Nov 2026.
notes: Whether the inheritance holds any retirement account is unknown.

claim: Life insurance proceeds and inheritances are not income to the recipient; later interest is
value: Not included in gross income
source: IRS - FAQ, Life insurance proceeds; California FTB - Gifts and inheritance
evidence: IRS: 'life insurance proceeds you receive as a beneficiary due to the death of the insured person, aren't includable in gross income'. FTB (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/file/personal/income-types/gifts-and-inheritance.html): 'If you received a gift or inheritance, do not include it in your income. However, if the gift or inheritance later produces income, you will need to pay tax on that income.' Both opened 11 Nov 2026.
notes: The IRS estate-tax page lists insurance among assets the gross estate may include.

claim: Deposit insurance treats a deceased owner's accounts as if the owner were alive for six months
value: Six months after death
source: FDIC - Your Insured Deposits
evidence: 'The FDIC insures a deceased person's accounts as if the person were still alive for six months after the death of the account holder.' Also: trust accounts at most $1,250,000 per owner at one bank from April 1, 2024. Opened 11 Nov 2026.

claim: A revocable trust that becomes irrevocable needs a new EIN; Form 56 notifies the IRS of a fiduciary; California Form 541 thresholds
value: Form 541: gross income over $10,000 or net income over $100
source: IRS - When to get a new EIN; IRS Topic no. 356; California FTB - Estates and trusts
evidence: IRS: 'Get a new EIN if you: ... Have a revocable trust that changes to an irrevocable trust.' Topic 356 (https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc356): 'You may need to file Form 56, Notice Concerning Fiduciary Relationship'. FTB (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/file/personal/filing-situations/estates-and-trusts/index.html): trusts, 'Gross income is over $10,000; Net income is over $100'. All opened 11 Nov 2026.

claim: Statutory compensation in a California probate, for the personal representative and again for the attorney
value: 4% of the first $100,000, 3% of the next $100,000, 2% of the next $800,000, 1% of the next $9,000,000, 0.5% of the next $15,000,000
source: California Probate Code sections 10800 and 10810
evidence: Section 10800(a)(1)-(5) and section 10810(a)(1)-(5) carry the same schedule; (b): 'the total amount of the appraisal value of property in the inventory ... without reference to encumbrances or other obligations on estate property'. Both opened 11 Nov 2026.
notes: Applies only to property that passes through probate.

claim: The 2026 initiative to restore the pre-2021 parent-child reassessment rule failed to qualify
value: Failure recorded 18 May 2026
source: California Secretary of State - advisories to county elections officials, May 2026 (CCROV #26138) & Nov 7, 2025 press release; Attorney General title and summary 25-0017
evidence: Advisory list and directly opened CCROV #26138 PDF (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/may/26138jh.pdf, May 18, 2026): 'Initiative: Failure of 1994, Related to Property Taxes on Transfers Between Family Members' ('the petition has failed'). Directly opened Nov 7, 2025 SOS news release links SOS #1994 and AG #25-0017 verbatim ('Allows transfers to children ... without property tax reassessment of: (1) principal residence, regardless of its current value or continued use as principal residence; and (2) $1 million in other real property').
notes: Current Proposition 19 rules stand.

claim: IRS rental, basis, home-sale, Form 706, 2026 trust brackets and portability documents opened directly
value: 27.5-year GDS; $25,000 passive allowance ($100,000-$150,000 MAGI); post-2008 nonqualified use; Form 706 Table A 40% over $1,000,000 ($345,800 base); 2026 trust 37% over $16,000 ($3,851 base); 5-year late portability under Rev. Proc. 2022-32
source: IRS Pubs. 527, 551, 523; Instructions for Form 706; Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026 trust rates); IRS Estate Tax FAQ; CDI Residential Insurance Guide
evidence: Opened directly 12 Nov 2026: Pub. 527 (https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527) Table 2-1 27.5 yrs GDS, $25,000 allowance phaseout $100,000-$150,000 MAGI; Pub. 551 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p551.pdf) gift basis and California community property step-up; Pub. 523 (https://www.irs.gov/publications/p523) Worksheet 3 post-2008 nonqualified use & post-May 6, 1997 depreciation; i706 (https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i706) Table A $345,800 + 40% over $1,000,000; Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf) Table 5 Estates & Trusts 2026 $3,851 + 37% over $16,000; IRS Estate FAQ (https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/frequently-asked-questions-on-estate-taxes) Rev. Proc. 2022-32 5-year portability route; CDI Residential Guide (https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/105-type/95-guides/03-res/res-ins-guide.cfm) 60+ day vacancy exclusion.
notes: All six IRS topics and the CDI guide (which superseded the Spanish fact sheet) were directly opened and read on 12 Nov 2026. Note the standalone f1041es.pdf URL returned a PDF fetch error; the authoritative statutory 2026 IRC sec. 1(j)(2)(E) Estates & Trusts table is directly verified in Rev. Proc. 2025-32 Section 4.01 Table 5 (alongside 2027 Rev. Proc. 2026-35).

claim: California Department of Insurance 2026 homeowners premium survey: hypothetical 40-year-old home in the Cupertino survey location, $2,500 deductible, at three dwelling limits
value: $500,000 dwelling: 35 of 37 insurers show a premium, from $790 to $3,371. $750,000 dwelling: 35 of 37, from $1,167 to $4,901. $1,000,000 dwelling: 35 of 37, from $1,543 to $6,430.
source: California Department of Insurance - 2026 Homeowners Insurance comparison tool, result pages for survey profiles 374, 376 and 377
evidence: Each result page states: 'All premiums displayed on this page are annual premiums and are effective as of May 1, 2026. This is not an insurance premium quote.' The page for each dwelling limit lists the same 37 insurers; two of them show no premium at the $2,500 deductible.
notes: A hypothetical home, not Property A. The middle of each list (this project's calculation, rounded to $10) is about $1,380, $2,020 and $2,690. The $500,000 and $750,000 pages are reached by changing the amount at the end of the link. Read by session 60ca3e1f; every row is transcribed in research/60ca3e1f/build_insurance_survey.py.

claim: Same survey: hypothetical 70-year-old home in the Cupertino survey location, $1,000,000 dwelling limit, $2,500 deductible
value: 34 of 36 insurers show a premium, from $1,598 to $4,968.
source: California Department of Insurance - 2026 Homeowners Insurance comparison tool, result page for survey profile 387
evidence: Result page as above, premiums effective May 1, 2026; 'This is not an insurance premium quote.'
notes: A hypothetical home, not Property A. Middle of the list (calculated, rounded to $10): about $2,740.

claim: Same survey: hypothetical owner-occupied home in the San Francisco (Sunset District) survey location, $1,000,000 dwelling limit, $2,500 deductible
value: 40-year-old home: 35 of 37 insurers show a premium, from $1,328 to $10,384. 70-year-old home: 34 of 36, from $1,413 to $10,384.
source: California Department of Insurance - 2026 Homeowners Insurance comparison tool, result pages for survey profiles 377 and 387
evidence: Result pages as above, premiums effective May 1, 2026; 'This is not an insurance premium quote.' The profile list has homeowners, condominium, renters and earthquake profiles; none is for a rented building of two to four units.
notes: Context only for Property B, which needs a landlord policy. Middle of each list (calculated, rounded to $10): about $3,350 and $3,190.

claim: Same survey: earthquake cover for a single-family home (profile 901), yearly rate per $1,000 of coverage
value: Cupertino: 40 insurers listed; 19 show a rate, from 1.15 to 15.00; 13 sell through the California Earthquake Authority; 8 refer to footnotes. San Francisco (Sunset District): 19 show a rate, from 1.13 to 15.00; 13 through the Authority; 8 footnotes.
source: California Department of Insurance - 2026 comparison tool, earthquake result pages
evidence: The page explains the rate as a cost per thousand dollars of coverage and gives its own example: $2.40 per thousand on $250,000 of coverage is $600 a year.
notes: Middle of each list (calculated): 3.10 and 3.29. Earthquake cover is a separate policy and is not in the model.

claim: California FAIR Plan residential policies in force in the two ZIP codes, 30 September 2022 to 30 September 2026
source: California FAIR Plan - Key Statistics and Data, 'residential policies in force by ZIP Code' (file dated 20 October 2026)
evidence: Table rows for 95014 and 94122 and the Total row, columns 'Number of Policies' at 9/30/2022 to 9/30/2026; the published year-over-year percentages agree with the counts.
notes: The file gives no count of homes per ZIP code, so no share is stated.

claim: What a California homeowners policy generally leaves out, and what sets the dwelling limit
value: Generally not covered: flood, earthquake, earth movement and 'Losses to house vacant for 60 days or more'. The dwelling limit should be the cost to replace the home, not its market value.
source: California Department of Insurance - Residential Insurance: Homeowners and Renters (guide, revised January 2026), English edition
evidence: The guide's list of perils generally not covered includes 'Losses to house vacant for 60 days or more'. On the dwelling limit: it 'should be the amount it would cost to replace your home' and 'may have nothing to do with the purchase price or the current market value'. It also says an insurer that sells homeowners cover must offer earthquake cover, and that a FAIR Plan policy is a basic fire policy without liability or theft cover.
notes: Replaces the earlier reading from the Spanish edition of a fact sheet (N-12). A guide describes policies in general; the wording of the actual policy governs and was not read.

claim: Congressional Budget Office long-run projections of inflation and the 10-year Treasury rate (February 2026)
value: Consumer price index 2.3% a year on average for 2029-2030 and for 2031-2036; PCE price index 2.0%; 10-year Treasury notes 4.3% for 2029-2030 and 4.4% for 2031-2036; real GDP growth 1.8%.
source: Congressional Budget Office - The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036, By the Numbers; and Table 2-1 of the economic projections data file
evidence: 'The Economic Outlook, by Calendar Year' table: Consumer price index 2.3 and 2.3; PCE price index 2.0 and 2.0; 10-year Treasury notes 4.3 and 4.4; Real GDP 1.8 and 1.8 (annual averages 2029-2030 and 2031-2036).
notes: Closes the flag that the 2.3% and 4.4% figures had been read from secondary summaries. The model's recorded-data page uses 2.3% for prices and 4.5% for the safe part of the portfolio.

claim: Congressional Budget Office projection of national home prices (February 2026)
value: FHFA house price index, purchase only (1991 Q1 = 100): 438.0 in 2026, 451.0 in 2027, 500.7 in 2030 and 621.1 in 2036.
source: Congressional Budget Office - economic projections data file, sheet '2. Calendar Year' (February 2026 baseline forecast)
notes: From 438.0 to 621.1 over ten years is about 3.6% a year (this project's calculation). The model raises both homes 3.5% a year. The index is national and ends in 2036; it is not a projection for either ZIP code.

claim: Federal Reserve projections of 16 September 2026
value: Median PCE inflation 3.7% in 2026, 2.3% in 2027, 2.1% in 2028, 2.0% in 2029 and in the longer run; federal funds rate 4.1% at the end of 2026 and 3.2% in the longer run; real GDP growth 2.0% in the longer run.
source: Federal Reserve - Summary of Economic Projections, 16 September 2026, Table 1
evidence: Table 1 medians: 'PCE inflation | 3.7 | 2.3 | 2.1 | 2.0 | 2.0'; 'Federal funds rate | 4.1 | 4.1 | 3.9 | 3.6 | 3.2'; 'Change in real GDP | 2.3 | 2.4 | 2.2 | 2.1 | 2.0'.
notes: Inflation in 2026 is running well above the 2.7% the Congressional Budget Office projected in February 2026.

claim: Social Security Trustees long-range assumptions (2026 report)
value: Intermediate: consumer prices (CPI-W) 2.4% a year; average covered wage 3.57% a year, 1.14% after inflation; real interest rate 2.3% from 2044. Low-cost and high-cost price assumptions: 3.0% and 1.8%.
source: 2026 OASDI Trustees Report - section II.C, Table II.C1, Key Assumptions and Summary Measures for Long-Range (75-Year) Projections
evidence: Table II.C1: 'Annual percentage change in Consumer Price Index (CPI-W) | 2.4 | 3.0 | 1.8'; 'average OASDI covered wage (nominal) | 3.57 | 4.79 | 2.34'; '(real) | 1.14 | 1.74 | .53'; 'new-issue real interest rate (percent) for years 2044 and later | 2.3 | 2.8 | 1.8'. Measures apply to 2036-2100.
notes: The model raises costs and Property A's market rent 3% a year, between the price assumption and the wage assumption.

claim: Whether the Proposition 19 amount that starts on 16 February 2027 has been published
value: Not published as of 12 November 2026.
source: California State Board of Equalization - 2026 Letters To Assessors (list)
evidence: The list runs from 2026/001 to 2026/044. No title on the list concerns the amount. Letter 2026/026 is 'Proposition 19 Intergenerational Transfer Exclusion Frequently Asked Questions and Answers' (dated August 3, 2026); its cover letter says the value cap is 'the sum of the property's factored base year value plus $1 million (adjusted every two years)' and gives no new amount.
notes: The amount now in force applies to transfers through 15 February 2027 (P19-01). The site keeps the later amount blank. Only the cover letter of 2026/026 was read (2 of 11 sections); the enclosed questions and answers were not read in full. See P19-11 for when the last amount came out.

claim: When the Board of Equalization published the Proposition 19 amount now in force
value: 7 March 2025, about three weeks after it took effect on 16 February 2025.
source: California State Board of Equalization - News Release NR 25-02 (March 7, 2025)
evidence: 'Today, the California State Board of Equalization (BOE) released the new amount adjusting the $1 million exclusion for Proposition 19 intergenerational transfers occurring on February 16, 2025, through February 15, 2027. The BOE is required to calculate and publish the adjustment every other year based on the Federal Housing Finance Agency's House Price Index for California. ... the amount increased by 2.15 percent, from $1,022,600 to $1,044,586. ... The notice to County Assessors was issued today in Letter to Assessors No. 2025/009.'
notes: By the same timetable the amount that starts on 16 February 2027 may not be published before March 2027.

claim: Whether the Proposition 19 intergenerational value cap is adjusted annually or every other year
value: Every other year. The Board of Equalization's Proposition 19 page describes the limit as current taxable value plus $1,000,000 'as biennially adjusted'; Letter to Assessors 2026/026 defines the excluded amount as the factored base-year value plus $1 million, with the $1 million 'adjusted on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 thereafter'.
source: BOE Letter to Assessors 2026/026 (3 August 2026), definition 5, and the BOE Proposition 19 comparison table
evidence: LTA 2026/026, definition 5: 'The $1 million is adjusted on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 thereafter. Also known as the "value cap".' BOE Proposition 19 page, parent-child table: 'Value limit of current taxable value plus $1,000,000 (as biennially adjusted)'. The Santa Clara County Assessor page says 'adjusted annually beginning in 2023', which conflicts with both; it is listed on Flagged for Review.
notes: The model takes one step every second 16 February, which follows the Board. No household figure.

claim: San Francisco Measure H (Muni parcel tax): preliminary vote and official multifamily rate structure
value: Preliminary Nov 10 tally: 74.4% Yes (244,760 Yes / 84,209 No; certification due Dec 11, 2026). Multifamily residential rate: $249 base plus $0.195 per sq ft over 5,000 sq ft (cap $50,000), July 1, 2027 to June 30, 2042, inflation-indexed from July 1, 2028; rent-controlled pass-through up to 50% capped at $65 per unit for pre-June 1, 2027 base rents.
source: City and County of San Francisco - Ballot Title & Summary (Measure H); SF Department of Elections preliminary count (Nov 10, 2026); OEA Economic Impact Report
evidence: Ballot Title & Summary table: Single-Family $129 base (caps/adders above 3,000 and 5,000 sq ft); Multifamily Residential $249 base plus $0.195/sq ft over 5,000 sq ft (max $50,000); Non-Residential $799 base (max $400,000). 'Owners of rent-controlled residential units could pass through up to 50% of the tax to their tenants, capped at $65 per unit, if the initial base rent was set before June 1, 2027.' Opened 12 Nov 2026.
notes: Property B's building square footage is unconfirmed and election certification is pending Dec 11, 2026, so no parcel dollar amount is added to the baseline yet.
